title: Index by position, name and an explicit mask
outcome: Select and replace vector elements without confusing positions, exclusions and unknown masks.
mechanism:
R's ordinary vector positions start at one. A positive integer index selects positions, and repeating an index repeats an output value. Zero selects nothing. A negative index excludes positions. Do not mix positive and negative positions in the same ordinary index, except zeros, because retaining and excluding would conflict.

Names provide labels, but they are not a relational key enforced by R. Names can be duplicated, absent or out of date. Character indexing selects a named value and can return NA for a missing name on an atomic vector. Validate the name set when missing or duplicated identifiers would make a calculation ambiguous.

A logical index is another vector. TRUE retains an entry, FALSE excludes it and NA can produce an unknown output entry. If a predicate contains NA, x[predicate] may contain a placeholder whose originating value is not established by the predicate. A deliberate known-only mask avoids that ambiguity. which returns positions of true entries and drops unknown predicates, so it expresses a different missingness policy.

Replacement uses the same selection mechanism on the left side of <-. x[2] <- 99 replaces an existing position, while an out-of-range assignment can extend a vector and introduce missing gaps. A boundary check should reject extension if the operation means update an existing observation. Syntax convenience does not establish a safe update contract.

vocabulary.definition: One-based positions to retain, possibly repeated.
Selection by an exact name on an object.
A vector describing which positions to retain.

anatomy: Use x[c(1,3)] to retain positions, x[-2] to exclude the second, and x[c("A","C")] for names. Keep the mask length equal to the data length when it describes one decision per record. Validate any requested key before updating.

worked_examples.title: Order and duplicates are part of selection
worked_examples.code:
x <- c(A = 10, B = 20, C = 30)
selected <- x[c(3, 1, 1)]
stopifnot(identical(unname(selected), c(30, 10, 10)))
stopifnot(identical(names(selected), c("C", "A", "A")))
print(selected)
worked_examples.explanation: The requested output order is C, A, A, and duplication is preserved. This is positional extraction, not a unique-key set operation.

worked_examples.title: Unknown mask versus known-only selection
worked_examples.code:
x <- c(10, 20, 30)
mask <- c(TRUE, NA, FALSE)
raw <- x[mask]
known <- x[!is.na(mask) & mask]
stopifnot(identical(raw, c(10, NA_real_)), identical(known, 10))
print(list(raw = raw, known = known))
worked_examples.explanation: The first output preserves an unknown selected position. The second explicitly restricts selection to known TRUE predicates.
worked_examples.expected: raw contains 10 and NA; known contains 10.

exercises.prompt: Exclude the middle entry of c(2,4,6).
Select and update a validated named value.
exercises.hint: Check the requested name exists exactly once.
exercises.answer: With unique names A, B, updating B changes only that entry.
exercises.expected: With unique names A, B, updating B changes only that entry.

exercises.prompt: Diagnose mixing c(1,-2) as an index.
exercises.hint: Positive retention and negative exclusion are incompatible.
exercises.answer: Use one indexing policy, such as c(1,3) or -2.
exercises.expected: Use one indexing policy, such as c(1,3) or -2.

exercises.prompt: Explain why character names are not a validated join key.
exercises.answer: Check uniqueness and missing names explicitly before keyed alignment.
exercises.expected: Check uniqueness and missing names explicitly before keyed alignment.

reference:
stopifnot(identical(c(4, 8)[c(2, 2, 1)], c(8, 8, 4)))
stopifnot(identical(c(2, 4, 6)[-2], c(2, 6)))
x <- c(A = 1, B = 2)
key <- "B"
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(names(x)), key %in% names(x))
x[key] <- 9
stopifnot(identical(unname(x), c(1, 9)))
error <- tryCatch(
  {
    c(2, 4, 6)[c(1, -2)]; FALSE
  },
  error = function(e) TRUE
)
stopifnot(error, length(x[integer(0)]) == 0L)
stopifnot(anyDuplicated(c("A", "A")) > 0L)
cat("r-005 reference checks passed\n")
solution_explanation:
The requested output order is C, A, A, and duplication is preserved. This is positional extraction, not a unique-key set operation.

The first output preserves an unknown selected position. The second explicitly restricts selection to known TRUE predicates.

The reference catches the deliberately invalid mixed index so the remaining assertions can still run. That error-handling helper is explained in r-015. The selection mechanism does not depend on knowing the handler yet: positive positions retain, negative positions exclude, and those policies cannot be mixed in the illustrated index.
